The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma

One message is not enough. The filter needs every pairwise distance in the archive at once. The fix is the union bound again: if each of ∣Q∣|Q|∣Q∣ vectors fails with probability at most 2e−ε2n/62e^{-\varepsilon^2 n/6}2e−ε2n/6, then some vector fails with probability at most 2∣Q∣e−ε2n/62|Q|e^{-\varepsilon^2 n/6}2∣Q∣e−ε2n/6. Set that equal to the failure probability δ\deltaδ you can live with, and solve for nnn.

With numbers: an archive of 200 messages has 200⋅199/2=19,900200 \cdot 199/2 = 19{,}900200⋅199/2=19,900 pairs. You want every squared distance within 30% (ε=0.3\varepsilon = 0.3ε=0.3) with probability at least 95% (δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05). Before reading on, guess the order of magnitude of nnn: tens, hundreds, or thousands?

To keep the next formula readable, we put the 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​ inside the matrix: from now on, a random projection is x↦Wxx \mapsto Wxx↦Wx where every entry of W∈Rn,dW \in \mathbb R^{n,d}W∈Rn,d is independent N(0,1/n)N(0, 1/n)N(0,1/n) (a standard normal divided by n\sqrt nn​).

Lemma (Johnson-Lindenstrauss). Let QQQ be a finite set of nonzero vectors in Rd\mathbb R^dRd, let δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0, 1)δ∈(0,1), and let nnn be an integer such that

ε=6ln⁡(2∣Q∣/δ)n≤12.\varepsilon = \sqrt{\frac{6 \ln(2|Q|/\delta)}{n}} \le \frac12 .ε=n6ln(2∣Q∣/δ)​​≤21​.

Then, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over the choice of a random projection W∈Rn,dW \in \mathbb R^{n,d}W∈Rn,d,

sup⁡x∈Q∣∥Wx∥2∥x∥2−1∣≤ε.\sup_{x \in Q} \left| \frac{\|Wx\|^2}{\|x\|^2} - 1 \right| \le \varepsilon .x∈Qsup​​∥x∥2∥Wx∥2​−1​≤ε.
  • ∣Q∣|Q|∣Q∣ is how many vectors QQQ contains; for distances in an archive of mmm messages, QQQ is the set of differences xi−xjx_i - x_jxi​−xj​, i<ji < ji<j, and ∣Q∣=m(m−1)/2|Q| = m(m-1)/2∣Q∣=m(m−1)/2.
  • ln⁡\lnln is the natural logarithm.
  • sup⁡x∈Q\sup_{x \in Q}supx∈Q​ is the largest value over all xxx in QQQ (for a finite set it is just the maximum).
  • The definition of ε\varepsilonε can be turned around: the guarantee holds at accuracy ε\varepsilonε as soon as n≥6ln⁡(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2n \ge 6\ln(2|Q|/\delta)/\varepsilon^2n≥6ln(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2.

In one sentence: with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, a random projection to n=6ln⁡(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2n = 6\ln(2|Q|/\delta)/\varepsilon^2n=6ln(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2 numbers keeps every squared length in QQQ within a fraction ε\varepsilonε, and nnn does not depend on ddd.

Proof. WWW is (1/n)(1/\sqrt n)(1/n​) times a matrix with standard normal entries, so for each fixed x∈Qx \in Qx∈Q the one-vector lemma says ∣∥Wx∥2/∥x∥2−1∣>ε\big|\|Wx\|^2/\|x\|^2 - 1\big| > \varepsilon​∥Wx∥2/∥x∥2−1​>ε with probability at most 2e−ε2n/62e^{-\varepsilon^2 n/6}2e−ε2n/6 (this needs ε≤1/2\varepsilon \le 1/2ε≤1/2, which the hypothesis provides). By the union bound over the ∣Q∣|Q|∣Q∣ vectors, the probability that the supremum exceeds ε\varepsilonε is at most 2∣Q∣e−ε2n/62|Q|e^{-\varepsilon^2 n/6}2∣Q∣e−ε2n/6. With ε\varepsilonε as defined, ε2n/6=ln⁡(2∣Q∣/δ)\varepsilon^2 n/6 = \ln(2|Q|/\delta)ε2n/6=ln(2∣Q∣/δ), so 2∣Q∣e−ε2n/6=2∣Q∣⋅δ/(2∣Q∣)=δ2|Q|e^{-\varepsilon^2 n/6} = 2|Q| \cdot \delta/(2|Q|) = \delta2∣Q∣e−ε2n/6=2∣Q∣⋅δ/(2∣Q∣)=δ. ■\blacksquare■

Our archive, term by term:

import math
m, eps, delta = 200, 0.3, 0.05
Q = m * (m - 1) // 2
n = math.ceil(6 * math.log(2 * Q / delta) / eps ** 2)
print(Q, n)

It prints 19900 906. Nine hundred and six numbers per message instead of 50,000, and the guarantee covers all 19,900 distances at once. Notice what is not in the formula: ddd. The same 906 would do for a vocabulary of five million words. The dimension you need grows only with the logarithm of the number of distances you want to keep.

Here is the lemma at work on 30 random messages of about 20 words each, out of 50,000. The formula with ∣Q∣=435|Q| = 435∣Q∣=435 pairs gives n=651n = 651n=651; the code squeezes all 30 messages and reports the worst squared-distance distortion over the 435 pairs.

import math
import random
d, m, n = 50000, 30, 651
rng = random.Random(8)
msgs = [{rng.randrange(d): rng.randint(1, 5) for _ in range(20)}
        for _ in range(m)]
cols = {}
def col(j):
    if j not in cols:
        r = random.Random(j)
        cols[j] = [r.gauss(0, 1 / math.sqrt(n)) for _ in range(n)]
    return cols[j]
proj = [[sum(c * col(j)[i] for j, c in x.items())
         for i in range(n)] for x in msgs]
def sq(a, b):
    return sum((a.get(k, 0) - b.get(k, 0)) ** 2 for k in a | b)
worst = max(abs(math.dist(proj[i], proj[j]) ** 2
                / sq(msgs[i], msgs[j]) - 1)
            for i in range(m) for j in range(i))
print(round(worst, 3))

It prints 0.212, inside the promised 0.3.

Two warnings before we use this. First, the guarantee is about squared lengths; for lengths themselves, 1−ε≤∥Wx∥2/∥x∥2≤1+ε1 - \varepsilon \le \|Wx\|^2/\|x\|^2 \le 1 + \varepsilon1−ε≤∥Wx∥2/∥x∥2≤1+ε gives 1−ε≤∥Wx∥/∥x∥≤1+ε\sqrt{1-\varepsilon} \le \|Wx\|/\|x\| \le \sqrt{1+\varepsilon}1−ε​≤∥Wx∥/∥x∥≤1+ε​, a slightly tighter band. Second, and more important, the set QQQ must be fixed before WWW is drawn. The probability is over WWW for a given QQQ. If someone picks the messages after seeing WWW, they can pick two messages whose difference lies in the null space of WWW (it always has one, since n<dn < dn<d), and that distance is squeezed to 0. In the mail room this means: draw WWW once, keep it secret from senders, and the guarantee covers any batch of messages that does not depend on it.

[diagram:jl: built on the lesson page]

Random projection as code

RandomProjection(n, d, seed):
  W ← n × d matrix, each entry drawn independently from N(0, 1/n)
  output: x ↦ W x

JLDimension(|Q|, ε, δ):
  requires: 0 < ε ≤ 1/2
  output: ⌈ 6 ln(2|Q|/δ) / ε² ⌉

Cost. Drawing WWW takes O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) time and O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) space, or no stored space at all if each column is regenerated from its own seed, as in the snippets. Squeezing one message costs O(nd)O(nd)O(nd), or O(ns)O(ns)O(ns) for a message with sss nonzero counts (only sss columns are touched). Comparing two squeezed messages then costs O(n)O(n)O(n) instead of O(d)O(d)O(d). For the 200-message archive at n=906n = 906n=906 with about 60 words per message, squeezing everything is about 200⋅60⋅906≈10.9200 \cdot 60 \cdot 906 \approx 10.9200⋅60⋅906≈10.9 million multiplications, done once, with no fitting at all.

Build it yourself.

import math
import random

def draw(m, d, words, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [{rng.randrange(d): rng.randint(1, 5)
             for _ in range(words)} for _ in range(m)]

def column(j, n):
    rng = random.Random(j)
    return [rng.gauss(0, 1 / math.sqrt(n)) for _ in range(n)]

def jl_dimension(size_Q, eps, delta): ...
def project(msgs, n): ...
def sq_dist(a, b): ...
def max_distortion(msgs, proj): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert jl_dimension(19900, 0.3, 0.05) == 906
    assert jl_dimension(435, 0.3, 0.05) == 651
    msgs = draw(30, 50000, 20, 8)
    proj = project(msgs, 651)
    assert round(max_distortion(msgs, proj), 3) == 0.212
    proj = project(msgs, 100)
    assert round(max_distortion(msgs, proj), 3) == 0.52
    print("all asserts pass")
  1. Implement jl_dimension from the lemma.
  2. Implement project(msgs, n): messages are dictionaries from word index to count; build each squeezed message from the columns column(j, n) of the words it uses, generating each column once.
  3. Implement sq_dist for two dictionaries and max_distortion, the largest ∣∥Wxi−Wxj∥2/∥xi−xj∥2−1∣\big|\|Wx_i - Wx_j\|^2/\|x_i - x_j\|^2 - 1\big|​∥Wxi​−Wxj​∥2/∥xi​−xj​∥2−1​ over pairs. The asserts check you against the snippet above, and against n=100n = 100n=100, where the worst pair is distorted by more than half.
  4. Redraw the matrix twenty times (give column a second seed, for instance random.Random(j + 100000 * t) for draw ttt) and run max_distortion at n=651n = 651n=651 on the same thirty messages each time. How many of the twenty land under 0.3? How many does the lemma promise?

Sparse messages

Random projections keep distances, but they cannot give you the message back: n<dn < dn<d, so the null space is still there. Yet look at an actual message. Out of 50,000 word counts, a typical message has maybe 60 that are not zero. Writing down 50,000 numbers to record 60 of them is absurd.

The count of nonzero entries has a name. For x∈Rdx \in \mathbb R^dx∈Rd,

∥x∥0=∣{ i:xi≠0 }∣.\|x\|_0 = \big|\{\, i : x_i \neq 0 \,\}\big| .∥x∥0​=​{i:xi​=0}​.
  • { i:xi≠0 }\{\, i : x_i \ne 0\,\}{i:xi​=0} is the set of positions iii such that entry iii is not zero: the words the message actually uses.
  • ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ counts how many positions that set contains.
  • The subscript 0 is a convention: ∥x∥0\|x\|_0∥x∥0​ is not a true length (doubling xxx does not double it), but it sits naturally next to ∥x∥1\|x\|_1∥x∥1​ and ∥x∥2\|x\|_2∥x∥2​, which we meet in a moment.

In one sentence: ∥x∥0\|x\|_0∥x∥0​ is the number of distinct words in the message. A message is s-sparse when ∥x∥0≤s\|x\|_0 \le s∥x∥0​≤s. The message “free free free prize winner winner” has counts 3, 1 and 2 on three words and 0 on the other 49,997:

x = {"free": 3, "prize": 1, "winner": 2}
d = 50000
print(len(x), d - len(x))

It prints 3 49997: ∥x∥0=3\|x\|_0 = 3∥x∥0​=3, so this message is 3-sparse, and so is any message using at most three words.

An s-sparse message can obviously be stored without loss as sss pairs (word index, count). So why not do that? Because that representation is not a fixed linear squeeze: you have to see the whole message first to know which positions to keep. Compressed sensing asks for something stranger. Fix one matrix WWW with nnn rows, the same for every message, chosen before any message exists. Store y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx. Then recover every s-sparse xxx exactly. A linear squeeze can be computed on the fly: as the parser reads each word, it adds that word’s column of WWW to a running total of nnn numbers, and the 50,000-count vector is never built. This is also why the idea matters outside the mail room: a camera or a medical scanner can measure the nnn weighted sums directly, instead of measuring everything and throwing most of it away. The same works for a message that is sparse after a fixed change of basis, x=Uαx = U\alphax=Uα with UUU orthonormal and α\alphaα sparse, since Wx=(WU)αWx = (WU)\alphaWx=(WU)α.

How can that work, when we proved that every squeeze has a null space? Because exact recovery of every message was impossible, but we only ask for sparse ones. The null space contains no sparse vectors, if WWW is chosen well. Three results make this precise:

  1. If WWW has a property called the restricted isometry property, every sparse message can be recovered exactly from WxWxWx.
  2. The recovery can be computed in polynomial time, by a linear program.
  3. A random WWW has the property, with high probability, once nnn is of order sln⁡ds \ln dslnd.

[diagram:sparse: built on the lesson page]

The restricted isometry property

The idea first. A random projection keeps the lengths of a finite set of vectors. Compressed sensing needs more: it needs WWW to keep the length of every sparse vector, infinitely many of them. If it does, then no sparse vector is squeezed to zero, and that is exactly what recovery needs.

Definition (restricted isometry property). A matrix W∈Rn,dW \in \mathbb R^{n,d}W∈Rn,d is (ε,s)(\varepsilon, s)(ε,s)-RIP if for every x≠0x \neq 0x=0 with ∥x∥0≤s\|x\|_0 \le s∥x∥0​≤s,

∣∥Wx∥2∥x∥2−1∣≤ε.\left| \frac{\|Wx\|^2}{\|x\|^2} - 1 \right| \le \varepsilon .​∥x∥2∥Wx∥2​−1​≤ε.
  • “x≠0x \ne 0x=0 with ∥x∥0≤s\|x\|_0 \le s∥x∥0​≤s” is every nonzero s-sparse vector.
  • The fraction is the squared distortion of xxx, exactly as in the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.
  • An isometry keeps all lengths; “restricted” means we only ask for it on sparse vectors, and only up to a fraction ε\varepsilonε.

In one sentence: WWW is (ε,s)(\varepsilon, s)(ε,s)-RIP when it gets the squared length of every s-sparse vector right within a fraction ε\varepsilonε. The smallest such ε\varepsilonε for a given WWW and sss is its RIP constant.

A tiny example makes it concrete. Take a vocabulary of six words and n=3n = 3n=3. For the columns of WWW, take the six unit vectors that point at opposite vertex pairs of a regular icosahedron, (0,±1,φ)(0, \pm 1, \varphi)(0,±1,φ), (±1,φ,0)(\pm 1, \varphi, 0)(±1,φ,0), (φ,0,±1)(\varphi, 0, \pm 1)(φ,0,±1), divided by their length 1+φ2\sqrt{1 + \varphi^2}1+φ2​, where φ=(1+5)/2\varphi = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2φ=(1+5​)/2 is the golden ratio. Any two of these columns make the same angle, with ∣cos⁡∣=1/5≈0.447|\cos| = 1/\sqrt 5 \approx 0.447∣cos∣=1/5​≈0.447. For a 2-sparse xxx using words iii and jjj, ∥Wx∥2=x⊤Gx\|Wx\|^2 = x^\top G x∥Wx∥2=x⊤Gx where GGG is the 2×22 \times 22×2 table of dot products of columns iii and jjj, so the distortion is bounded by the two eigenvalues of GGG, here 1±0.4471 \pm 0.4471±0.447. Checking all 15 pairs:

from itertools import combinations
phi = (1 + 5 ** 0.5) / 2
raw = [(0, 1, phi), (0, -1, phi), (1, phi, 0),
       (-1, phi, 0), (phi, 0, 1), (phi, 0, -1)]
cols = [[t / (1 + phi ** 2) ** 0.5 for t in c] for c in raw]
dot = lambda a, b: sum(p * q for p, q in zip(a, b))
worst = 0.0
for i, j in combinations(range(6), 2):
    a, b, c = dot(cols[i], cols[i]), dot(cols[i], cols[j]), \
        dot(cols[j], cols[j])
    mid, gap = (a + c) / 2, (((a - c) / 2) ** 2 + b * b) ** 0.5
    worst = max(worst, abs(mid + gap - 1), abs(mid - gap - 1))
print(round(worst, 3), round(1 / (1 + 2 ** 0.5), 3))

It prints 0.447 0.414. So this 3×63 \times 63×6 matrix is (0.447,2)(0.447, 2)(0.447,2)-RIP. (The second number, 1/(1+2)1/(1 + \sqrt 2)1/(1+2​), will matter in two sections.) Keep this example in mind: six words, three stored numbers, and every message that uses one word.

Theorem (sparse messages are determined by their squeeze). Let ε<1\varepsilon < 1ε<1 and let WWW be (ε,2s)(\varepsilon, 2s)(ε,2s)-RIP. Let xxx be s-sparse, let y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx, and let

x~∈argmin⁡v : Wv=y∥v∥0\tilde x \in \operatorname*{argmin}_{v \,:\, Wv = y} \|v\|_0x~∈v:Wv=yargmin​∥v∥0​

be a reconstruction. Then x~=x\tilde x = xx~=x.

  • v:Wv=yv : Wv = yv:Wv=y ranges over every vector that squeezes to the stored yyy.
  • argmin⁡∥v∥0\operatorname{argmin} \|v\|_0argmin∥v∥0​ picks one of them with the fewest nonzero entries; the ∈\in∈ says there may be several tied, and x~\tilde xx~ is any one of them.

In one sentence: if WWW is RIP for twice the sparsity, the sparsest message that matches the stored numbers is the message itself. Note the “twice”: the proof compares two s-sparse vectors, and their difference can use 2s2s2s words.

Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that x~≠x\tilde x \ne xx~=x. The true xxx itself satisfies Wx=yWx = yWx=y, so it is one of the candidates, and the sparsest candidate can be no less sparse: ∥x~∥0≤∥x∥0≤s\|\tilde x\|_0 \le \|x\|_0 \le s∥x~∥0​≤∥x∥0​≤s. The difference x−x~x - \tilde xx−x~ is nonzero only where xxx or x~\tilde xx~ is, so ∥x−x~∥0≤2s\|x - \tilde x\|_0 \le 2s∥x−x~∥0​≤2s, and the RIP inequality applies to it. But W(x−x~)=y−y=0W(x - \tilde x) = y - y = 0W(x−x~)=y−y=0, so its squared distortion ratio is 0, and the RIP inequality reads ∣0−1∣≤ε|0 - 1| \le \varepsilon∣0−1∣≤ε, that is, 1≤ε1 \le \varepsilon1≤ε. This contradicts ε<1\varepsilon < 1ε<1. ■\blacksquare■

In the icosahedron example, s=1s = 1s=1 and WWW is (0.447,2)(0.447, 2)(0.447,2)-RIP, so every 1-sparse message is determined by its three stored numbers. Here is the sparsest-candidate search for the message “2.5 times word 3”: for a 1-sparse candidate, yyy must be a multiple of a single column, so the code tries each column.

phi = (1 + 5 ** 0.5) / 2
raw = [(0, 1, phi), (0, -1, phi), (1, phi, 0),
       (-1, phi, 0), (phi, 0, 1), (phi, 0, -1)]
cols = [[t / (1 + phi ** 2) ** 0.5 for t in c] for c in raw]
dot = lambda a, b: sum(p * q for p, q in zip(a, b))
x = [0, 0, 0, 2.5, 0, 0]
y = [sum(cols[j][r] * x[j] for j in range(6)) for r in range(3)]
for j, w in enumerate(cols):
    c = dot(y, w)
    if max(abs(a - c * b) for a, b in zip(y, w)) < 1e-9:
        print("word", j, "count", round(c, 6))
print([round(t, 3) for t in y])

It prints word 3 count 2.5 and the stored numbers [-1.314, 2.127, 0.0]. Exactly one column fits, so exactly one 1-sparse message squeezes to these three numbers, as the theorem says.

The catch is the search. For six words and s=1s = 1s=1 there are six candidate supports. For 50,000 words and messages of 60 words, the number of possible sets of 60 words is (5000060)≈1.0×10200\binom{50000}{60} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{200}(6050000​)≈1.0×10200. Minimizing ∥v∥0\|v\|_0∥v∥0​ is a combinatorial search, and no computer will finish it.

import math
print(math.comb(6, 1), f"{math.comb(50000, 60):.1e}")

It prints 6 1.0e+200: six supports to try in the tiny example, a one followed by two hundred zeros in the mail room.

Recovery by a linear program

Here is the surprising part. Replace the count of nonzero entries by the sum of absolute values,

∥v∥1=∑i=1d∣vi∣,\|v\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^d |v_i| ,∥v∥1​=i=1∑d​∣vi​∣,

the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm of vvv. (For the message above with counts 3, 1 and 2, ∥x∥1=6\|x\|_1 = 6∥x∥1​=6; for comparison ∥x∥0=3\|x\|_0 = 3∥x∥0​=3 and the ordinary length is ∥x∥2=∥x∥=14\|x\|_2 = \|x\| = \sqrt{14}∥x∥2​=∥x∥=14​.) In one sentence: the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm is the total of the counts, ignoring signs. Minimizing it over all vvv with Wv=yWv = yWv=y is a convex problem, and in fact a linear program: introduce one extra variable tit_iti​ per word and solve

min⁡v, t∈Rd  ∑i=1dtisuch thatWv=y,  −ti≤vi≤ti for every i.\min_{v,\, t \in \mathbb R^d} \; \sum_{i=1}^d t_i \quad\text{such that}\quad Wv = y,\; -t_i \le v_i \le t_i \text{ for every } i .v,t∈Rdmin​i=1∑d​ti​such thatWv=y,−ti​≤vi​≤ti​ for every i.

At the optimum each tit_iti​ is pushed down to ∣vi∣|v_i|∣vi​∣, so the objective is ∥v∥1\|v\|_1∥v∥1​: for v=(3,−1,2)v = (3, -1, 2)v=(3,−1,2) the smallest allowed ttt is (3,1,2)(3, 1, 2)(3,1,2), total 6. Linear programs can be solved in polynomial time (lesson 9 used one to find a separating halfspace). The question is whether the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ minimizer is still the true message. It is, under a slightly stronger RIP, and we can even say what happens for messages that are only nearly sparse.

For an arbitrary xxx, let xsx_sxs​ be the vector that keeps the sss entries of xxx largest in absolute value and sets the rest to 0: the best s-sparse approximation of xxx. Then ∥x−xs∥1\|x - x_s\|_1∥x−xs​∥1​ is the total of the small entries, how far xxx is from being s-sparse. For the message with counts (3,1,2)(3, 1, 2)(3,1,2) and s=2s = 2s=2, xsx_sxs​ keeps 3 and 2 and ∥x−xs∥1=1\|x - x_s\|_1 = 1∥x−xs​∥1​=1. Here are the three ways of measuring that message, and its small-entry total, term by term:

import math
x = [3, 1, 2]
s = 2
l0 = sum(t != 0 for t in x)
l1 = sum(abs(t) for t in x)
l2 = math.sqrt(sum(t * t for t in x))
kept = sorted(x, key=abs, reverse=True)[:s]
tail = l1 - sum(abs(t) for t in kept)
print(l0, l1, round(l2, 3), tail)

It prints 3 6 3.742 1: three words, a total of six counts, a length of 14≈3.742\sqrt{14} \approx 3.74214​≈3.742, and a total of 1 outside the two biggest entries.

Theorem (ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ recovery). Let ε<11+2\varepsilon < \frac{1}{1 + \sqrt 2}ε<1+2​1​ and let WWW be (ε,2s)(\varepsilon, 2s)(ε,2s)-RIP. Let xxx be an arbitrary vector, y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx, and

x⋆∈argmin⁡v : Wv=y∥v∥1.x^\star \in \operatorname*{argmin}_{v \,:\, Wv = y} \|v\|_1 .x⋆∈v:Wv=yargmin​∥v∥1​.

Then

∥x⋆−x∥2≤2 1+ρ1−ρ s−1/2 ∥x−xs∥1,ρ=2 ε1−ε.\|x^\star - x\|_2 \le 2\, \frac{1 + \rho}{1 - \rho}\, s^{-1/2}\, \|x - x_s\|_1, \qquad \rho = \frac{\sqrt 2\, \varepsilon}{1 - \varepsilon}.∥x⋆−x∥2​≤21−ρ1+ρ​s−1/2∥x−xs​∥1​,ρ=1−ε2​ε​.
  • x⋆x^\starx⋆ is the output of the linear program: the matching vector with the smallest total.
  • ∥x⋆−x∥2\|x^\star - x\|_2∥x⋆−x∥2​ is the ordinary length of the recovery error.
  • ρ\rhoρ is a number built from ε\varepsilonε; the condition ε<1/(1+2)\varepsilon < 1/(1+\sqrt 2)ε<1/(1+2​) is exactly what makes ρ<1\rho < 1ρ<1, since 2ε<1−ε\sqrt 2 \varepsilon < 1 - \varepsilon2​ε<1−ε rearranges to ε(1+2)<1\varepsilon(1 + \sqrt 2) < 1ε(1+2​)<1.
  • s−1/2=1/ss^{-1/2} = 1/\sqrt ss−1/2=1/s​.

In one sentence: the linear program recovers any message up to an error proportional to the part of it that is not s-sparse; in particular, it recovers every s-sparse message exactly, because then x=xsx = x_sx=xs​ and the right-hand side is 0. With ε=0.3\varepsilon = 0.3ε=0.3:

eps = 0.3
rho = 2 ** 0.5 * eps / (1 - eps)
C = 2 * (1 + rho) / (1 - rho)
print(round(rho, 3), round(C, 2))

It prints 0.606 8.15: a (0.3,2s)(0.3, 2s)(0.3,2s)-RIP matrix recovers an almost-sparse message with error at most 8.15/s8.15/\sqrt s8.15/s​ times its small-entry total. For s=2s = 2s=2 and the (3,1,2)(3, 1, 2)(3,1,2) message, that is at most 8.15⋅1/2≈5.88.15 \cdot 1/\sqrt 2 \approx 5.88.15⋅1/2​≈5.8, and exactly 0 if the message had used only two words.

The proof is the longest in this lesson, so here is its plan. Write h=x⋆−xh = x^\star - xh=x⋆−x for the error. Split the ddd positions into blocks of sss. Show that the part of hhh outside the two most important blocks is small, using only the fact that x⋆x^\starx⋆ has the smallest ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm (Claim 1). Show that the part inside those two blocks is small, using the RIP (Claim 2). Add.

Notation. For a vector vvv and a set of positions III, vIv_IvI​ is the vector equal to vvv on III and 0 elsewhere. [d]={1,…,d}[d] = \{1, \dots, d\}[d]={1,…,d} is the set of all positions, and Ic=[d]∖II^c = [d] \setminus IIc=[d]∖I is the set of positions not in III. For v=(5,−1,2)v = (5, -1, 2)v=(5,−1,2) and I={1,3}I = \{1, 3\}I={1,3}, vI=(5,0,2)v_I = (5, 0, 2)vI​=(5,0,2) and vIc=(0,−1,0)v_{I^c} = (0, -1, 0)vIc​=(0,−1,0). We assume d/sd/sd/s is a whole number to keep the blocks equal; nothing changes otherwise except that the last block is smaller.

The blocks. Let T0T_0T0​ be the sss positions where ∣xi∣|x_i|∣xi​∣ is largest (ties broken arbitrarily), so xT0=xsx_{T_0} = x_sxT0​​=xs​ and xT0c=x−xsx_{T_0^c} = x - x_sxT0c​​=x−xs​. Let T1T_1T1​ be the sss positions outside T0T_0T0​ where ∣hi∣|h_i|∣hi​∣ is largest, T2T_2T2​ the next sss positions by ∣hi∣|h_i|∣hi​∣ outside T0∪T1T_0 \cup T_1T0​∪T1​, and so on until every position is used. Write T0,1=T0∪T1T_{0,1} = T_0 \cup T_1T0,1​=T0​∪T1​.

Lemma (RIP makes disjoint sparse vectors nearly perpendicular). Let WWW be (ε,2s)(\varepsilon, 2s)(ε,2s)-RIP. For any two disjoint sets I,JI, JI,J of at most sss positions each, and any vector uuu,

∣⟨WuI,WuJ⟩∣≤ε ∥uI∥ ∥uJ∥.|\langle W u_I, W u_J \rangle| \le \varepsilon\, \|u_I\|\, \|u_J\| .∣⟨WuI​,WuJ​⟩∣≤ε∥uI​∥∥uJ​∥.

Here ⟨a,b⟩=a⋅b\langle a, b \rangle = a \cdot b⟨a,b⟩=a⋅b is the dot product. Before the squeeze, uIu_IuI​ and uJu_JuJ​ are exactly perpendicular, because they have no position in common. In one sentence: after an RIP squeeze, vectors on disjoint sets of words stay nearly perpendicular, with a cosine at most ε\varepsilonε.

Proof. Both sides scale the same way, so assume ∥uI∥=∥uJ∥=1\|u_I\| = \|u_J\| = 1∥uI​∥=∥uJ​∥=1. For any vectors, ⟨a,b⟩=14(∥a+b∥2−∥a−b∥2)\langle a, b \rangle = \frac14 \big(\|a + b\|^2 - \|a - b\|^2\big)⟨a,b⟩=41​(∥a+b∥2−∥a−b∥2) (expand both squares; the ∥a∥2\|a\|^2∥a∥2 and ∥b∥2\|b\|^2∥b∥2 terms cancel). With a=WuIa = Wu_Ia=WuI​ and b=WuJb = Wu_Jb=WuJ​, and since uI±uJu_I \pm u_JuI​±uJ​ uses at most 2s2s2s positions and has squared length ∥uI∥2+∥uJ∥2=2\|u_I\|^2 + \|u_J\|^2 = 2∥uI​∥2+∥uJ​∥2=2 (disjoint supports, so Pythagoras), the RIP gives 2(1−ε)≤∥W(uI±uJ)∥2≤2(1+ε)2(1 - \varepsilon) \le \|W(u_I \pm u_J)\|^2 \le 2(1 + \varepsilon)2(1−ε)≤∥W(uI​±uJ​)∥2≤2(1+ε). So

⟨WuI,WuJ⟩≤14(2(1+ε)−2(1−ε))=ε,⟨WuI,WuJ⟩≥14(2(1−ε)−2(1+ε))=−ε.\langle Wu_I, Wu_J\rangle \le \tfrac14\big(2(1 + \varepsilon) - 2(1 - \varepsilon)\big) = \varepsilon, \qquad \langle Wu_I, Wu_J\rangle \ge \tfrac14\big(2(1 - \varepsilon) - 2(1 + \varepsilon)\big) = -\varepsilon.⟨WuI​,WuJ​⟩≤41​(2(1+ε)−2(1−ε))=ε,⟨WuI​,WuJ​⟩≥41​(2(1−ε)−2(1+ε))=−ε.

■\blacksquare■

On the icosahedron matrix (s=1s = 1s=1, ε=0.447\varepsilon = 0.447ε=0.447), every pair of distinct single-word vectors should have ∣⟨WuI,WuJ⟩∣/(∥uI∥∥uJ∥)≤0.447|\langle Wu_I, Wu_J\rangle| / (\|u_I\|\|u_J\|) \le 0.447∣⟨WuI​,WuJ​⟩∣/(∥uI​∥∥uJ​∥)≤0.447:

import random
phi = (1 + 5 ** 0.5) / 2
raw = [(0, 1, phi), (0, -1, phi), (1, phi, 0),
       (-1, phi, 0), (phi, 0, 1), (phi, 0, -1)]
cols = [[t / (1 + phi ** 2) ** 0.5 for t in c] for c in raw]
dot = lambda a, b: sum(p * q for p, q in zip(a, b))
rng = random.Random(5)
ratio = 0.0
for _ in range(10000):
    i, j = rng.sample(range(6), 2)
    a, b = rng.gauss(0, 1), rng.gauss(0, 1)
    wa, wb = [a * t for t in cols[i]], [b * t for t in cols[j]]
    ratio = max(ratio, abs(dot(wa, wb)) / abs(a * b))
print(round(ratio, 3))

It prints 0.447: the bound is met with equality, because these columns all meet at the same angle.

The split. By the triangle inequality, ∥h∥=∥hT0,1+hT0,1c∥≤∥hT0,1∥+∥hT0,1c∥\|h\| = \|h_{T_{0,1}} + h_{T_{0,1}^c}\| \le \|h_{T_{0,1}}\| + \|h_{T_{0,1}^c}\|∥h∥=∥hT0,1​​+hT0,1c​​∥≤∥hT0,1​​∥+∥hT0,1c​​∥. We will show

which is the theorem. (The first step uses Claim 1 and ∥hT0∥≤∥hT0,1∥\|h_{T_0}\| \le \|h_{T_{0,1}}\|∥hT0​​∥≤∥hT0,1​​∥, the second Claim 2, and the last puts 4ρ+2(1−ρ)=2(1+ρ)4\rho + 2(1 - \rho) = 2(1 + \rho)4ρ+2(1−ρ)=2(1+ρ) over 1−ρ1 - \rho1−ρ.)

Claim 1, the tail is small. This uses no RIP at all, only that x⋆x^\starx⋆ has the smallest ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm.

∥hTj∥≤s1/2 ∥hTj∥∞≤s−1/2 ∥hTj−1∥1.\|h_{T_j}\| \le s^{1/2}\, \|h_{T_j}\|_\infty \le s^{-1/2}\, \|h_{T_{j-1}}\|_1 .∥hTj​​∥≤s1/2∥hTj​​∥∞​≤s−1/2∥hTj−1​​∥1​.

∥hT0,1c∥≤∑j≥2∥hTj∥≤s−1/2∑j≥1∥hTj∥1=s−1/2 ∥hT0c∥1.\|h_{T_{0,1}^c}\| \le \sum_{j \ge 2} \|h_{T_j}\| \le s^{-1/2} \sum_{j \ge 1} \|h_{T_j}\|_1 = s^{-1/2}\, \|h_{T_0^c}\|_1 .∥hT0,1c​​∥≤j≥2∑​∥hTj​​∥≤s−1/2j≥1∑​∥hTj​​∥1​=s−1/2∥hT0c​​∥1​.

In one sentence: the length of everything past the first two blocks is at most the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ total outside T0T_0T0​, divided by s\sqrt ss​. Here is this inequality tested on 10,000 random vectors with d=12d = 12d=12, s=3s = 3s=3 (the code takes the first three positions as T0T_0T0​ and sorts the rest into blocks); the printed number is the largest ratio of the left side to the right side and must be at most 1:

import random
rng = random.Random(6)
d, s = 12, 3
norm2 = lambda v: sum(t * t for t in v) ** 0.5
worst = 0.0
for _ in range(10000):
    h = [rng.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(d)]
    rest = sorted(h[s:], key=abs, reverse=True)
    blocks = [rest[k:k + s] for k in range(0, len(rest), s)]
    tail = norm2([t for b in blocks[1:] for t in b])
    l1 = sum(abs(t) for t in rest)
    worst = max(worst, tail / (l1 / s ** 0.5))
print(round(worst, 3))

It prints 0.453.

Step 2d is where ε<1/(1+2)\varepsilon < 1/(1 + \sqrt 2)ε<1/(1+2​) is needed: with ρ≥1\rho \ge 1ρ≥1 the inequality says nothing. Our icosahedron matrix has ε=0.447\varepsilon = 0.447ε=0.447, just above the threshold 0.414, so this theorem does not cover it, even though the earlier theorem does. You will find in the build-it challenge that the linear program recovers its 1-sparse messages anyway: the RIP condition is sufficient, not necessary.

Random matrices have the property

The last piece: where do RIP matrices come from? Checking the RIP of a given matrix means checking every set of 2s2s2s columns, which is the same impossible search as before. So we do not check. We draw WWW at random and prove that it is RIP with high probability.

The idea in words. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma handles a finite set of vectors. The sparse vectors on one fixed set III of sss words form a whole subspace, infinitely many vectors. But it is enough to control a finite net of them, a set of unit vectors so dense that every unit vector of the subspace is close to one of them, and then bootstrap from the net to everything. Finally, take a union bound over all (ds)\binom{d}{s}(sd​) choices of III.

Lemma (a finite net of the sphere). For every ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon \in (0, 1]ε∈(0,1] and every sss, there is a set NNN of unit vectors in Rs\mathbb R^sRs with ∣N∣≤(1+2/ε)s|N| \le (1 + 2/\varepsilon)^s∣N∣≤(1+2/ε)s such that every unit vector of Rs\mathbb R^sRs is within distance ε\varepsilonε of some point of NNN.

In one sentence: about (3/ε)s(3/\varepsilon)^s(3/ε)s points are enough to come within ε\varepsilonε of every direction in sss dimensions. In two dimensions with ε=0.25\varepsilon = 0.25ε=0.25, the bound allows (1+8)2=81(1 + 8)^2 = 81(1+8)2=81 points.

Proof. Build NNN greedily: keep adding a unit vector at distance more than ε\varepsilonε from all points chosen so far, until none is left. If some unit vector were farther than ε\varepsilonε from every point of NNN, we could have added it, so when the process stops, NNN has the covering property. It does stop, and the count is bounded, by a volume argument: points of NNN are more than ε\varepsilonε apart, so the balls of radius ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2 around them do not overlap; and since the centres have length 1, all these balls lie inside the ball of radius 1+ε/21 + \varepsilon/21+ε/2 around the origin. A ball of radius rrr in Rs\mathbb R^sRs has volume csrsc_s r^scs​rs for a constant csc_scs​. Comparing volumes, ∣N∣ cs(ε/2)s≤cs(1+ε/2)s|N|\, c_s (\varepsilon/2)^s \le c_s (1 + \varepsilon/2)^s∣N∣cs​(ε/2)s≤cs​(1+ε/2)s, so ∣N∣≤(1+2/ε)s|N| \le (1 + 2/\varepsilon)^s∣N∣≤(1+2/ε)s. ■\blacksquare■

The greedy construction on the circle:

import math
eps = 0.25
net = []
for k in range(100000):
    t = 2 * math.pi * k / 100000
    p = (math.cos(t), math.sin(t))
    if all(math.dist(p, q) > eps for q in net):
        net.append(p)
far = max(min(math.dist((math.cos(t), math.sin(t)), q)
              for q in net)
          for t in [2 * math.pi * k / 997 for k in range(997)])
print(len(net), round((1 + 2 / eps) ** 2), far <= eps)

It prints 25 81 True: 25 points cover the circle to within 0.25, well under the bound of 81.

Lemma (one sparse subspace). Let UUU be an orthonormal d×dd \times dd×d matrix, let III be a set of sss positions, and let SSS be the span of the columns UiU_iUi​, i∈Ii \in Ii∈I. Let δ,ε∈(0,1)\delta, \varepsilon \in (0, 1)δ,ε∈(0,1) and let nnn satisfy

n≥24 ln⁡(2/δ)+sln⁡(12/ε)ε2.n \ge 24\, \frac{\ln(2/\delta) + s \ln(12/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^2} .n≥24ε2ln(2/δ)+sln(12/ε)​.

Then, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over a random projection W∈Rn,dW \in \mathbb R^{n,d}W∈Rn,d, every nonzero x∈Sx \in Sx∈S has ∣ ∥Wx∥/∥x∥−1∣≤ε\big|\, \|Wx\|/\|x\| - 1 \big| \le \varepsilon​∥Wx∥/∥x∥−1​≤ε.

In one sentence: a random projection with a few times sln⁡(1/ε)/ε2s\ln(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2sln(1/ε)/ε2 rows keeps the length of every vector in one fixed s-dimensional subspace within a fraction ε\varepsilonε. For the messages that use two given words (s=2s = 2s=2), with ε=0.5\varepsilon = 0.5ε=0.5 and δ=0.01\delta = 0.01δ=0.01:

import math

The bootstrap. Let aaa be the smallest number such that ∥Wx∥≤(1+a)∥x∥\|Wx\| \le (1 + a)\|x\|∥Wx∥≤(1+a)∥x∥ for every x∈Sx \in Sx∈S; it is finite because WWW restricted to SSS is a linear map on a finite-dimensional space. grid = [k / 1000 for k in range(1, 1001)]

Theorem (random matrices are RIP). Let UUU be a fixed orthonormal d×dd \times dd×d matrix, let ε,δ∈(0,1)\varepsilon, \delta \in (0, 1)ε,δ∈(0,1), let s∈[d]s \in [d]s∈[d], and let

n≥216 ln⁡(2/δ)+sln⁡(36 d/ε)ε2.n \ge 216\, \frac{\ln(2/\delta) + s\ln(36\, d/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^2} .n≥216ε2ln(2/δ)+sln(36d/ε)​.

Then, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over a random projection W∈Rn,dW \in \mathbb R^{n,d}W∈Rn,d, the matrix WUWUWU is (ε,s)(\varepsilon, s)(ε,s)-RIP.

In one sentence: a random projection with a constant times sln⁡(d/ε)/ε2s \ln(d/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2sln(d/ε)/ε2 rows is RIP for sparsity sss, in the standard basis and in any other fixed orthonormal basis. The dependence on ddd is only logarithmic, which is the whole point: nnn of order sln⁡ds \ln dslnd, not ddd.

Proof. Apply the subspace lemma to every set III of exactly sss positions, with accuracy ε/3\varepsilon/3ε/3 and confidence δ/(ds)\delta/\binom dsδ/(sd​). There are (ds)≤ds\binom ds \le d^s(sd​)≤ds such sets, so the lemma needs n≥24⋅9 (ln⁡(2(ds)/δ)+sln⁡(36/ε))/ε2n \ge 24 \cdot 9\, \big(\ln(2\binom ds/\delta) + s\ln(36/\varepsilon)\big)/\varepsilon^2n≥24⋅9(ln(2(sd​)/δ)+sln(36/ε))/ε2, and since ln⁡(ds)≤sln⁡d\ln \binom ds \le s\ln dln(sd​)≤slnd, the hypothesis is enough. By the union bound, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ all the subspaces succeed at once. Every s-sparse α≠0\alpha \ne 0α=0 has its nonzero entries inside some III of size sss, so WUαWU\alphaWUα lies in that subspace and 1−ε/3≤∥WUα∥/∥α∥≤1+ε/31 - \varepsilon/3 \le \|WU\alpha\|/\|\alpha\| \le 1 + \varepsilon/31−ε/3≤∥WUα∥/∥α∥≤1+ε/3. Squaring, the squared ratio lies between 1−2ε/3+ε2/9≥1−ε1 - 2\varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon^2/9 \ge 1 - \varepsilon1−2ε/3+ε2/9≥1−ε and 1+2ε/3+ε2/9≤1+ε1 + 2\varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon^2/9 \le 1 + \varepsilon1+2ε/3+ε2/9≤1+ε (the last because ε2/9≤ε/3\varepsilon^2/9 \le \varepsilon/3ε2/9≤ε/3). That is the RIP. ■\blacksquare■

To recover messages of 60 words we need (ε,2s)(\varepsilon, 2s)(ε,2s)-RIP with ε<0.414\varepsilon < 0.414ε<0.414, so s=120s = 120s=120 in this theorem. Let’s see what it asks for, with ε=0.4\varepsilon = 0.4ε=0.4 and δ=0.01\delta = 0.01δ=0.01:

import math
d, s, eps, delta = 50000, 60, 0.4, 0.01
k = 2 * s
n = 216 * (math.log(2 / delta) + k * math.log(36 * d / eps))
n /= eps ** 2
print(f"{n:.2e}", round(n / d))

It prints 2.49e+06 50: two and a half million rows, fifty times more than the 50,000 counts we started with. Be honest about what this means. The theorem’s shape, sln⁡ds \ln dslnd, is the real phenomenon; its constant 216 is the price of a proof built from a crude net and a union bound over 1020010^{200}10200 subsets, and it is far too large to certify anything at the mail room’s size. Sharper analyses exist with much smaller constants, but they are beyond this lesson. What this lesson certifies at practical sizes is the random projection of the previous section, and that is what you will use to fix the bug.

Compressed sensing as code

Encode(W, x):
  W is n × d, drawn once
  output: y ← W x

DecodeSparsest(W, y, s):
  exact when W is (ε, 2s)-RIP with ε < 1
  for k = 0, 1, …, s:
    for every set I of k positions:
      if some v supported on I has W v = y: output v

DecodeL1(W, y):
  exact when W is (ε, 2s)-RIP with ε < 1/(1+√2)
  solve the linear program
    minimize Σ_i t_i  over v, t ∈ ℝ^d
    subject to W v = y,  −t_i ≤ v_i ≤ t_i  for every i
  output: v

Cost. Encoding costs O(nd)O(nd)O(nd), or O(ns)O(ns)O(ns) for an s-sparse message. DecodeSparsest tries up to ∑k≤s(dk)\sum_{k \le s}\binom dk∑k≤s​(kd​) supports, each a small least-squares solve of cost O(nk2)O(nk^2)O(nk2): exponential in sss. DecodeL1 is a linear program with 2d2d2d variables and n+2dn + 2dn+2d constraints, solvable in time polynomial in nnn and ddd. So squeezing is as cheap as a random projection and all the price is in the decoder, a trade that pays when you squeeze far more often than you decode.

Build it yourself. The icosahedron matrix, six words, three stored numbers. For decode_l1, use a fact from the theory of linear programs: when the minimum exists, it is reached at a solution with at most nnn nonzero entries whose columns are linearly independent. So for this tiny problem you may enumerate every set of n=3n = 3n=3 columns, solve the 3×33 \times 33×3 system, and keep the solution with the smallest ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm.

from itertools import combinations

phi = (1 + 5 ** 0.5) / 2
raw = [(0, 1, phi), (0, -1, phi), (1, phi, 0),
       (-1, phi, 0), (phi, 0, 1), (phi, 0, -1)]
cols = [[t / (1 + phi ** 2) ** 0.5 for t in c] for c in raw]

def measure(cols, x):
    return [sum(cols[j][r] * x[j] for j in range(len(cols)))
            for r in range(len(cols[0]))]

def l0_norm(x): ...
def rip_constant_pairs(cols): ...
def solve(M, y): ...
def decode_l0(cols, y, s): ...
def decode_l1(cols, y): ...

def close(a, b):
    return max(abs(p - q) for p, q in zip(a, b)) < 1e-9

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert l0_norm([0, 2.5, 0, -1, 0, 0]) == 2
    assert round(rip_constant_pairs(cols), 3) == 0.447
    for j in range(6):
        for c in (2.5, -1, 7):
            x = [0.0] * 6
            x[j] = c
            y = measure(cols, x)
            assert close(decode_l0(cols, y, 1), x)
            assert close(decode_l1(cols, y), x)
    print("all asserts pass")
  1. Implement l0_norm and rip_constant_pairs, the RIP constant for 2s=22s = 22s=2, from the eigenvalues of each 2×22 \times 22×2 table of column dot products.
  2. Implement solve(M, y), Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting that returns None for a singular system.
  3. Implement decode_l0 (try supports of size 1 up to sss, solve least squares on each, accept an exact match) and decode_l1 (the enumeration above). The asserts check all 18 one-word messages.
  4. Now take a two-word message, x=(1,0,0,2,0,0)x = (1, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0)x=(1,0,0,2,0,0). Is the matrix (ε,4)(\varepsilon, 4)(ε,4)-RIP for any ε<1\varepsilon < 1ε<1? (Think about four vectors in R3\mathbb R^3R3.) Find two different two-word messages with the same three stored numbers, and then see what decode_l1 returns for xxx. What does that tell you about recovery that works on one message but has no guarantee?

PCA or compressed sensing?

You now have two ways to squeeze with a promise of recovery, and they rest on different assumptions about the messages.

PCA assumes the messages lie near a low-dimensional subspace. It recovers perfectly whenever the archive lies exactly in an nnn-dimensional subspace, and it is the best linear squeeze with linear recovery for the archive you fit it on.

Compressed sensing assumes the messages are sparse, in some known basis. It recovers perfectly every s-sparse message, from about sln⁡ds \ln dslnd numbers, with a nonlinear decoder.

Each wins where the other’s assumption fails. The single-word messages e1,…,ede_1, \dots, e_de1​,…,ed​ are 1-sparse, so compressed sensing recovers them all from order ln⁡d\ln dlnd numbers, where PCA loses most of each one. In the other direction, take mmm messages that lie exactly in an nnn-dimensional subspace. PCA recovers them perfectly with nnn numbers. They are also nnn-sparse in any orthonormal basis whose first nnn vectors span the subspace, so compressed sensing works too, but it needs on the order of nln⁡dn \ln dnlnd numbers, and with exactly nnn it can fail. For the mail room, word counts are sparse and do not lie near a small subspace, so compressed sensing’s assumption is the right one for recovering messages, and a random projection is the right tool for keeping distances. If all you need is the best summary of a fixed archive, for instance to plot it or to find its main themes, PCA is the right one.

Fix the bug

Back to the slow mail room. The nearest-neighbour filter needs the distances between this week’s messages, and your manager wants a promise, not a hope: every one of the pairwise squared distances among this week’s 200 messages must stay within 30% of its true value (ε=0.3\varepsilon = 0.3ε=0.3), with probability at least 95% (δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05). The budget is at most 1,000 stored numbers per message. And there is a rule of the house: the squeeze is chosen on Monday morning, before this week’s messages arrive, and each message is squeezed as soon as it comes in.

You have two candidates. PCA, fitted on last week’s 200 messages, with up to 199 components. Or a random projection, with nnn of your choice. Before you open the lab, decide which one the theory can certify and which nnn it needs. Then think about this: the lab also shows the measured worst distortion on this week’s actual messages, and at n=500n = 500n=500 it happens to come out at 0.243, under 0.3. Is n=500n = 500n=500 good enough?

[lab-act2: built on the lesson page]

Measuring is not certifying. At n=500n = 500n=500 the Johnson-Lindenstrauss bound on the failure probability is 2⋅19,900 e−0.09⋅500/6≈222 \cdot 19{,}900\, e^{-0.09 \cdot 500/6} \approx 222⋅19,900e−0.09⋅500/6≈22, which promises nothing (a probability bound above 1 is no bound). The draw you see happened to be fine; next week’s draw has no such promise. Only n≥906n \ge 906n≥906 carries the 95% guarantee, and it fits the budget. PCA cannot be certified at all: its components are mixes of last week’s messages, which used about 10,700 of the 50,000 words, and on average almost four fifths of each new message’s squared length falls on words outside them and is lost.

What people get wrong

“PCA is the best way to reduce dimension.” It is the best linear squeeze with linear recovery, measured by total squared error, on the archive it was fitted to. With a nonlinear decoder, sparse messages can be recovered from far fewer numbers than PCA needs, and for messages outside the archive PCA promises nothing.

“A random matrix loses information at random, so it must be worse than a fitted one.” For keeping distances, the random projection is the one that comes with a guarantee for messages it has never seen, and its dimension depends on how many distances you keep, not on ddd. Its weakness is different: the messages must not be chosen after seeing WWW.

“The Johnson-Lindenstrauss dimension grows with the number of words.” There is no ddd in n=6ln⁡(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2n = 6\ln(2|Q|/\delta)/\varepsilon^2n=6ln(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2. Doubling the vocabulary changes nothing; doubling the archive adds about 6ln⁡4/ε26 \ln 4/\varepsilon^26ln4/ε2 rows.

“Exact recovery of a squeezed message is impossible.” It is impossible for every message, because of the null space. It is possible for every sparse message, when the null space contains no sparse vectors, which is what the RIP for 2s2s2s guarantees.

“If the linear program recovered my test messages, the matrix is fine.” Success on the messages you tried is not a guarantee for the next one. In the build-it challenge the linear program recovers a two-word message from three numbers, yet some two-word messages are indistinguishable from each other at that size, so no decoder can recover them all.

“The constants in the RIP theorem tell you how many measurements you need.” They give a number that certainly suffices, from a crude proof; the sln⁡ds \ln dslnd shape is the lesson, the 216 is not.

Recap and the next bug

  1. A compression matrix W∈Rn,dW \in \mathbb R^{n,d}W∈Rn,d squeezes a message into nnn weighted sums; with n<dn < dn<d its null space makes exact recovery of every message impossible.
  2. PCA minimizes the total squared round-trip error over linear squeezes and recoveries. The best pair is W=U⊤W = U^\topW=U⊤ with orthonormal columns, the columns are the eigenvectors of the scatter matrix A=∑ixixi⊤A = \sum_i x_i x_i^\topA=∑i​xi​xi⊤​ for its nnn largest eigenvalues, and the error left over is the sum of the discarded eigenvalues. When d≫md \gg md≫m, eigenvectors of the m×mm \times mm×m Gram matrix XX⊤XX^\topXX⊤ give the same components at cost O(m3+m2d)O(m^3 + m^2 d)O(m3+m2d).
  3. A random projection with N(0,1/n)N(0, 1/n)N(0,1/n) entries keeps the squared length of any one fixed vector within ε\varepsilonε except with probability 2e−ε2n/62e^{-\varepsilon^2 n/6}2e−ε2n/6 (for ε≤1/2\varepsilon \le 1/2ε≤1/2), by chi-squared concentration and Chernoff’s method. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma adds a union bound: n=6ln⁡(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2n = 6\ln(2|Q|/\delta)/\varepsilon^2n=6ln(2∣Q∣/δ)/ε2 numbers keep a whole set QQQ, independently of ddd.
  4. Compressed sensing: an (ε,2s)(\varepsilon, 2s)(ε,2s)-RIP matrix determines every s-sparse message; with ε<1/(1+2)\varepsilon < 1/(1+\sqrt 2)ε<1/(1+2​) a linear program recovers it, and almost-sparse messages approximately. A random matrix with order sln⁡(d/ε)/ε2s\ln(d/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2sln(d/ε)/ε2 rows is RIP with high probability, by a net, the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma and a union bound.
  5. PCA bets on a subspace, compressed sensing on sparsity. The mail room’s word counts are sparse, and its distances are best kept by a random projection certified by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.

The filter is fast again. At the Friday review, though, a colleague from the statistics team looks at everything you have built this term and frowns. Every learner so far, she says, draws a boundary between junk and keep: a halfspace, a tree, a neighbourhood. None of them says anything about how a junk message comes to be written. Why not model that instead? Describe how a junk message is produced, word by word, and how a keep message is produced, learn both descriptions from the archive, and when a new message arrives, ask which of the two most likely produced it. Is that a better idea than drawing a boundary, or a worse one? That is the next lesson: generative models.

Concept check

Write your answers down before moving on to the next lesson, with your reasoning, not just the answer.

  1. All six messages of a new archive lie on the plane where the “meeting” count is exactly 1 (so the plane does not pass through the origin), and the messages are not all on one line. Is uncentered PCA with n=2n = 2n=2 exact on this archive, meaning total error 0? Is PCA with n=2n = 2n=2 exact after centering? Use the formula for the leftover error, and say what you must store besides the two numbers per message in the centered case.
  2. In the proof of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, the union bound runs over the vectors of QQQ. Where does the proof use that QQQ is fixed before WWW is drawn? Show that the conclusion can fail completely if a sender may choose two messages after seeing WWW, whatever n<dn < dn<d is.
  3. Your archive grows to 1,000 messages and you want all pairwise squared distances within 25% with probability at least 99%. How many numbers per message does the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma ask for? What changes if the vocabulary grows from 50,000 to five million words? And for messages of 60 words out of 50,000, why can you not use this lesson’s RIP theorem to justify recovering them from that many numbers?

Problems

Once the concept check is done, try these. Hints come one at a time in the chat, and no full solutions.

  • Problem 1 (PCA as maximizing variance).
